cards.front: (Linear algebra) Definition: $\mathbf v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$ when …
cards.extra: The zero vector is excluded: it would satisfy the equation for every $\lambda$.

cards.front: Which equation do the eigenvalues of $A$ solve?

cards.back: $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf v = \mathbf 0$ has a non-zero solution exactly when $A - \lambda I$ is singular, i.e. its determinant is 0.

cards.text: The sum of the eigenvalues equals the {{c1::trace}}; their product equals the {{c2::determinant}}.

cards.extra: $\det(A-\lambda I)$ of a triangular matrix is the product of $(a_{ii} - \lambda)$.

cards.front: $A$ is singular. Which eigenvalue must it have?
cards.back: $0$, because $A\mathbf v = \mathbf 0 = 0\cdot\mathbf v$ for some $\mathbf v \neq \mathbf 0$.

cards.front: If $A\mathbf v = \lambda\mathbf v$, what is $A^k\mathbf v$?
$A$ is invertible with eigenpair $(\lambda, \mathbf v)$. An eigenpair of $A^{-1}$?

cards.back: $\ker(A - \lambda I)$: all eigenvectors for $\lambda$ together with $\mathbf 0$

cards.text: {{c1::Algebraic}} multiplicity counts $\lambda$ as a root of the characteristic polynomial; {{c2::geometric}} multiplicity is $\dim E_\lambda$.

cards.front: When is an $n\times n$ matrix diagonalisable?
cards.back: Exactly when it has $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors (equivalently, geometric = algebraic multiplicity for every eigenvalue).

cards.front: Standard example of a non-diagonalisable $2\times 2$ matrix?
cards.back: The shear $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$: eigenvalue 1 twice, but only one eigenvector direction.

cards.front: Two facts about the eigen-structure of a real symmetric matrix?
cards.back: All eigenvalues are real, and there is an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors (spectral theorem).
